subject: biology-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.stem: Which feature of capillaries makes them suitable for exchange?
choices: Thick muscular walls that withstand pressure
Valves that prevent the backflow of blood
Walls one cell thick, sometimes with pores
Elastic fibres that recoil after each heartbeat
items.note: Thin, permeable walls and a large total surface area allow exchange with tissues.

items.stem: Arteries have thick walls with elastic and muscle tissue because they:
choices: Carry blood at high pressure away from the heart
Carry blood at low pressure back to the heart
Exchange materials with the body's tissues
Contain valves to stop blood flowing backward
items.note: Elastic fibres stretch and recoil, maintaining pressure; muscle adjusts diameter.

items.stem: Water is carried from roots to leaves in:
choices: Phloem sieve tubes
Xylem vessels
Companion cells
Guard cells
items.note: Xylem conducts water and minerals; phloem transports sugars (translocation).

choices: Blood pressure is high, so valves slow the blood
Valves help to oxygenate the blood
Valves pump blood back to the heart
Blood pressure is low, so valves stop backflow
items.note: Low pressure in veins could let blood flow backwards; valves and skeletal muscle contractions keep it moving to the heart.

items.stem: A coronary occlusion is dangerous because it:
choices: Stops blood leaving the left ventricle into the aorta
Causes the valves of the heart to close permanently
Prevents the lungs from receiving any oxygen
Blocks blood supply to heart muscle, depriving it of oxygen
items.note: Blocked coronary arteries starve cardiac muscle of oxygen; the tissue can die (heart attack).

items.stem: In the cohesion–tension theory, water is pulled up the xylem because:
choices: Root cells pump water molecules upward through the xylem by active transport
Phloem pushes water up as sugars are loaded
Evaporation from leaves creates tension, and cohesion holds the column together
Water is attracted upward by sunlight
items.note: Transpiration pulls water (tension); hydrogen bonds (cohesion) and adhesion to xylem walls keep the column continuous.

items.stem: The pulse felt in an artery is caused by:
choices: A surge of blood at high pressure each time the ventricles contract
The closing of valves in the veins near the skin
The rhythmic contraction of smooth muscles in the artery wall itself
The blood returning to the atria between beats
items.note: Each ventricular contraction sends a pressure wave along the arteries.

items.stem: Tissue fluid forms at the arterial end of a capillary because:
choices: Plasma proteins leave the capillary and pull water out
Hydrostatic pressure is higher than the osmotic pull of plasma proteins
Active transport by endothelial cells pumps plasma out of the capillary
Osmotic pressure is higher than hydrostatic pressure
items.note: High pressure forces fluid out; at the venous end, pressure drops and water returns by osmosis. Excess drains into lymph.

choices: The atrioventricular valves close and the semilunar valves open
The atrioventricular valves open and the semilunar valves close
Both sets of valves are open
Blood flows from the atria into the ventricles
items.note: Ventricles contract: pressure shuts AV valves (first heart sound) and opens semilunar valves into arteries.

items.stem: Translocation in phloem moves sucrose from source to sink because:
choices: Sucrose diffuses down its gradient through the xylem
Loading of sucrose at the source draws in water, and the pressure pushes sap to the sink
Transpiration pulls sap from leaves towards the roots
Companion cells contract rhythmically and squeeze the sap along the sieve tubes towards the roots
items.note: Mass flow: loading lowers water potential at the source; water enters from xylem; hydrostatic pressure drives flow to the sink.

choices: Evaporation of water from the leaves pulling the whole water column upward
Cohesion between water molecules in the xylem
Active transport of mineral ions into the xylem, followed by osmosis
Contraction of cells in the root cortex
items.note: Ions pumped into the xylem lower water potential; water follows by osmosis, building pressure (important in spring, before leaves open).

items.stem: Compare the structure of arteries and veins.
markscheme: Both have three layers / a lumen lined with endothelium (1)
Arteries have thicker walls with more muscle and elastic tissue (1)
Veins have valves; arteries do not (except at the heart) (1)
items.tactic: Compare: one similarity, then paired differences with reasons if asked.

items.stem: Explain how water moves from the soil into the xylem of a root.
markscheme: Root hair cells have a large surface area (1)
Mineral ions actively transported into root cells, lowering water potential (1)
Water moves in by osmosis and passes across the cortex to the xylem (1)
items.tactic: Follow the water: soil → root hair → cortex → xylem, with the mechanism at each step.

items.stem: Describe the events of the cardiac cycle from atrial systole to diastole.
markscheme: Atria contract, pushing blood into the ventricles (AV valves open) (1)
Ventricles contract; AV valves close; semilunar valves open; blood enters arteries (1)
Ventricles relax; semilunar valves close as arterial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure (1)
Atria fill with blood from veins during diastole (1)
items.tactic: Sequence with valve positions at each stage: valves move because of pressure differences.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) Water uptake by a leafy shoot was measured with a potometer under four conditions (mm³ min⁻¹): still air 20 °C 12; moving air 20 °C 21; still air 30 °C 19; still air 20 °C with leaves coated in grease on lower surfaces 3.
(a) Calculate the percentage increase caused by moving air. (b) Explain the effect of greasing the lower surfaces. (c) State why a potometer measures water uptake rather than transpiration directly.
markscheme: (b) Most stomata are on the lower surface; grease blocks them so little water vapour is lost (1)
Less transpiration means less tension, so uptake falls (to 3) (1)
(c) Some water taken up is used in photosynthesis / to keep cells turgid (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
